newsitem.title: SPAIN: INTERVIEW - Rejuvenated BCH to expand more in Latam.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Rejuvenated BCH to expand more in Latam.

text.p: Spain's Banco Central Hispano has put hard times behind it and is planning more purchases to complete its banking network in Latin America, board member and general manager Antonio Escamez said.
"We are putting the era of suffering behind us. BCH is taking off," Escamez told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.

BCH, Spain's fourth-largest bank and the product of the 1991 merger of Banco Central and Banco Hispanoamericano, has pursued a sweeping restructuring and rationalisation plan to purge its balance sheet of loan problems that is now paying off.
According to restructuring plans, the bank is aiming for a 25 percent rise in net profit in 1997 over 1996. First-half earnings are due on July 24.
In 1996, BCH reported net profit of 44.09 billion, more than double 1995's results after heavy restructuring charges.

Despite its woes, BCH has invested some $500 million this decade to become the biggest banker in Chile and take a key stake in Mexico's Grupo Bital, building on a presence in the region stretching back to the early 1960s.

One of a trio of Spanish banks that have been aggressively expanding in Latin America in the past few years, BCH also has banks in Paraguay, Uruguay, Peru and Argentina through its alliance with the Chilean Luksic group.
But the bank is by no means content.
"There is no doubt that we do not have the map completed that we want to have in that area," Escamez said.
This spring its plans for a Colombian purchase, with a stake in the Banco de Colombia, fell through.
"In places where we have no presence or just a small one, such as Colombia, we would like to have a presence. (But) at the moment we are not negotiating anything in Colombia.
"We will not be carrying out any operations in Colombia or any other place the rest of this year as we would like to consolidate (our holdings) more," he said.
In addition, he said BCH was interested possibly in the markets of Brazil, Venezuela and in Central America.
The Bank's international holdings, predominantly in Latin America, should contribute to earnings as its volume to assets dictates, he said.
At present, BCH's foreign holding contribute some 30 percent to overall earnings and could rise to up to 40 percent short-term.
"The contribution to earnings should reflect volume ...Between 30 and 40 percent would be good short-term," he said.
The group has said a rebound in earnings would be reflected in payouts to shareholders, which have suffered duing the restructing.
On 1996 earnings, the group paid a total dividend of 110 pesetas gross a share. On 1995 earnings, it paid out a gross 75 pesetas, charged to reserves, following 125 pesetas in 1994.
"If there is a rise in earnings. It's logical that this will be reflected in shareholder payouts but I don't know by how much," Escamez said.
